items.originalTitle: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise
items.author: Samuel Benson, Myah Ward and Eric Bazail-Eimil
items.title: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise
items.summary: In the days before the midterm election, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) felt confident that a blue wave could open the door to immigration reform. Cuellar was so bullish that he reached out to acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement director David Venturella and the Customs and Border Protection commissioner Rodney Scott to feel out areas of “common ground,” he said in an interview. Now Cuellar is one of several moderate Democrats angling to strike a deal with the White House, especially on reining in ICE officers and creating legal pathways to citizenship for some immigrants. They’re undeterred by President Donald Trump’s elevation of immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff. And they’re buoyed by Trump’s recent admission that his deportations policy was “too tough.” Several of these Democrats have already placed calls to Trump and DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin to express a willingness to work together. Cuellar said he reached back out to Venturella and Scott after the election to try to schedule meetings. “If the president, as the president of the United States, makes a decision — and not a chief of staff — we can get the job done,” Cuellar said in an interview. “I’m sure we’re going to find a lot of differences, but if we sit down, we can definitely resolve them.” It’ll be a tough road: Securing buy-in from the White House becomes undoubtedly more complicated with Miller, a champion of the administration’s aggressive deportation push. Republicans in Congress have largely been willing to defer to the president on the issue. And Democratic leaders have questioned Trump’s sincerity and said they have no interest in working with Miller. The possibility will become even more tenuous once Democrats begin investigating the Trump administration, including the president’s immigration enforcement agencies. CBP and ICE did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did Democratic leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries. Democrats like Cuellar, Sen.-elects James Talarico of Texas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina are aware of all of those hurdles. But they’re betting the midterms have created an opening for serious talks: Latino voters across the country swung hard back toward Democrats this cycle, and more and more Republicans are recognizing that their immigration agenda hurt them politically. Talarico and Andrews have publicly expressed interest in working with the president on immigration, and both ran on platforms that emphasized creating paths to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. “I’m ready to work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system,” Talarico said in a statement. Inside the White House, there’s a recognition that the president will proceed however he so chooses, regardless of who the chief of staff is. Trump is accessible to outside voices — journalists, business leaders and lawmakers regularly call him directly — and often poses policy questions to aides and allies as he decides which direction he will go. “Everybody’s like, ‘Well, it’s never going to happen with Stephen Miller.’ Look, Donald Trump’s the president. I don’t care if Stephen Miller’s the chief of staff or Susie Wiles or John Kelly or whoever the chief of staff might be,” said a person close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak about the internal dynamic. For Democrats, there’s a real political incentive to getting a deal done ahead of a critical 2028 presidential election — especially as the party seeks to win back voter trust on immigration and border security, policy areas that spelled doom for them in 2024. “You have these Democrats who flip red states, and it’s also to their self-interest, right? Not just to do rhetoric, and go big or go home, but actually come to the middle with the president, with the Republicans. Because if not, I think that the big lesson this election is, Hispanic voters are gonna flip back ... if they don’t see Democrats delivering anything the next two years,” said Rebecca Shi, the executive director of ABIC, a coalition of pro-immigration reform business executives. She added that there’s a lesson for Republicans, too, if they don’t come to the table: “They will lose the White House.” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis touted Trump’s immigration accomplishments, including border security, a drop in crime and the creation of the Homeland Security Task Force and said the president’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.” She said Democrats should work alongside Trump to “keep our southern border secure, remove dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and stop the illicit trafficking of lethal drugs.” Democrats welcomed the president’s remarks on 60 Minutes on Sunday, when he said he was open to legal pathways for some unauthorized immigrants who haven’t committed crimes and are working and contributing to the economy. Mullin also floated an openness to a bipartisan immigration overhaul involving DACA, which could provide permanent legal status to some undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, even as he — and the president — have insisted that any proposal wouldn’t include amnesty. In a sign that Democrats have learned the lessons of the Biden administration , many of them are eager to pair reforms with border security measures. Cuellar, who will chair the Homeland Security Appropriations subcommittee in the next conference, has long suggested including guardrails on ICE in the next funding bill, such as requiring judicial warrants, rolling out body camera usage and restoring “sensitive locations” such as churches and schools as off-limits. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), another Democrat who has expressed interest in working with the Trump administration, said that beyond “talk,” it would help to see some smaller concrete policy shifts from the White House to affirm that Trump is, in fact, open to changes to the immigration system. “The way to do that is to have some reforms already at ICE — whether it’s shutting down these detention centers, giving certain level of protections, whether to veterans, so they don't get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. citizens, they don’t get deported — something to show that, you know, it's not just talk, this isn’t going to be a policy led by Stephen Miller,” he said. But Miller remains a bogeyman for Democrats, someone they view as responsible for the president’s most extreme immigration policies. As chief of staff, he can ensure he’s one of the last people in the president’s ear — and that the White House doesn’t bend to what he sees as unrealistic Democratic demands. “The reason why they wouldn’t do an amnesty deal, I believe, is because it would be the ultimate and most public contradiction of the central thesis of this entire political program as it was sold to voters,” said Mike Howell, president of the Oversight Project and a member of the Mass Deportation Coalition. “It would be the end of the America First coalition as it currently exists.” Democrats' distrust of Miller will also make it challenging for them to align on any potential deal with the White House. “Stephen Miller is the mastermind and architect of terror, and death, and illegality in this country, and he is not anyone who even understands truthfully what immigration policy should look like,” said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif). “No deals, man. No deals,” she added. The White House pointed to Miller’s experience on the Hill as a valuable asset. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said unlike Democrats “who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C. and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance.” Lawmakers are waiting for the president to make the first move. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead his fellow Republicans when Democrats retake control of the Senate this January, told reporters after the election that “if there's something he wants to do there, we can have that conversation.” “There are always some landmines, which is why in the past the wheels have kind of come off, despite some really good efforts at trying to find a landing spot. But yeah we're open to something he wants to propose,” Thune added. Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: Is a Manual Treadmill Worth the Extra Effort?
items.author: Jennifer Heimlich
items.title: Is a Manual Treadmill Worth the Extra Effort?
items.summary: —MDV Edwards—Getty Images You’re at the gym facing a line of treadmills . Most are your standard running machine with an electric motor and a flat deck. But there are also a few odd looking machines that arch up in the front and the back, with no buttons on the console and no plug for an outlet. Meet the manual treadmill, also called a self-powered or non-motorized treadmill. These machines are designed with a curved surface so that as you land from each stride, the force of your foot moving downward revolves the belt around the deck. Each step you take powers the treadmill. (There are also some flat manual treadmills, though they’re far less common and generally used only for walking.) In CrossFit gyms and Reddit threads alike, you’ll come across plenty of runners who say manual treadmills are better for you. “A lot of people think that the motorized treadmill is doing all the work, and because of that, they have to use a non-motorized treadmill to really get the benefits of running ,” says Richard Willy, an associate professor in the school of health and rehabilitation sciences at The Ohio State University. Experts say that’s largely a misconception—yet there are other good reasons to hop on a manual treadmill. How manual treadmills work your body differently The most common argument for manual treadmills is that they help you run with a more natural gait, closer to how you’d run on a road or a track. But a 2023 study in the Journal of Sports Sciences found that traditional treadmills actually do a better job of replicating outdoor running than manual ones do. “There's very little difference between running on a motorized treadmill and running overground,” Willy says. The curve of a manual treadmill changes the joint movements in the lower body, explains Mohammad Saad, a physical therapist with Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City. The thighs lift higher, putting the hips in a more flexed position, while the ankles go through a bigger range of motion, and the knees stay in a more flexed position the entire time. With this gait, the mechanical load shifts away from the knee joints and more onto the hips and ankles. And because runners have to use the force of their stride to accelerate the belt, they tend to use their propulsive muscles—the calves, hamstrings, and glutes—more, according to Willy. He says this can make manual treadmills helpful for people with knee pain, but dicey for those with glute, hamstring, calf, or Achilles problems. Meanwhile, research also shows that runners also tend to run with a shorter stride and higher cadence (meaning more steps per minute) on a manual treadmill. These two patterns are generally linked to more efficient running, though it hasn’t yet been studied if this gait style translates when a runner steps off the treadmill and heads out the door. Biomechanics aside, there’s also the effort level to consider: A manual treadmill makes for a brutal workout. Multiple studies have found it takes significantly more energy to run on these machines compared to motorized treadmills. “The metabolic cost can be anywhere from 16-38% more,” Saad says. Runners use up more oxygen and calories, their heart rate spikes higher, they breathe heavier, and the same pace feels harder. This is partially because of the extra energy it takes to move the belt, and partly because that curved surface means you’re basically running uphill nonstop. “It's the equivalent of running on about a five-degree incline the whole time,” says James Smoliga, a professor in the department of rehabilitation sciences at Tufts University who led a 2015 study comparing the intensities on manual and motorized treadmills. Although there’s been far less research on walking on a non-motorized treadmill, the trends are similar: Smoliga’s study found that even for healthy, athletic adults, walking on the curved, manual treadmill used up so much energy it qualified as a “vigorous” workout by American College of Sports Medicine standards. (That can be good or bad, depending on your goals.) So why do many runners think manual treadmills feel more natural? That likely has more to do with the mental challenge of running than any physical effects. On a traditional treadmill, you key in the pace you want, then just have to keep up. But on a manual treadmill, your body sets the pace with each stride, so you have to keep focused and continually check in to stay on target—just like you would outside. Practicing this can help runners prepare for the cognitive effort it takes to maintain a certain speed on race day. “You can do your entire workout based on your own feeling of intensity, which is a valuable part of training,” Smoliga says. The best way to use a manual treadmill It’s not unheard of for runners to do the bulk of their workouts on motorized treadmills. Recently, professional runner Vincent Mauri placed 10th in the Chicago Marathon after doing about 70% of his training on standard treadmills at his local Planet Fitness. “You just don't hear about people doing that on a non-motorized treadmill, and that's because the metabolic cost is too high,” Willy says. Manual treadmills are best used as specialized tools for short, hard efforts like sprints or fast intervals. Saad, for instance, says he typically only hops on a manual treadmill for one to four minutes at a time in his own training. “If you're looking to have a very intense workout in a very short period of time, a curved, non-motorized treadmill is the way to go,” Willy says. While it’s technically possible to do a long endurance run on a manual treadmill, just know that doing, say, a 10-miler on this machine will tax your body far more than running 10 miles on the road or a motorized treadmill. You’ll essentially be running 10 miles uphill the entire time while also pushing against the resistance of the belt. For this reason, Smoliga cautions runners to generally ignore their pace on manual treadmills and instead run by effort, listening to their bodies. He also warns beginners that these machines take some time to get used to. Step too far forward, and the belt starts whizzing underneath you; too far back, and it barely moves. “It takes practice to get to the point where you can maintain a consistent pace,” Smoliga says. Although they call for different approaches, Smoliga emphasizes that both machines can be valuable training tools. Choosing which to hop on just depends on your goals for that day’s run. “I don't think one treadmill is better or worse than the other,” Smoliga says. “They do slightly similar but different things, and each has their place.”

items.originalTitle: Philippine Protests Grow as Government Welcomes Trump
items.author: Chad de Guzman
items.title: Philippine Protests Grow as Government Welcomes Trump
items.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is welcomed upon his arrival at Villamor Air Base in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. —Win McNamee—Getty Images When Donald Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday for the first stop of his trip to Asia this week , the Philippine government rolled out the red carpet for the ally leader. But elsewhere in the Southeast Asian nation, the U.S. President’s welcome wasn’t so warm. In the lead-up to Trump’s visit, activists, students, and members of the local indigenous community clashed with Philippine law enforcement in the capital, where the 2026 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit is being hosted, and in Cebu . The demonstrations have repeated the demand: “Trump Out.” Violence and commotion can be seen in videos and photos shared online by local journalists. On Sunday, more than 200 people were arrested. The protests erupted as the Philippines opened the ASEAN Summit on Sunday and invited several world leaders to Manila. Civic groups have condemned the response from the Philippine police, which has insisted it exercised “maximum tolerance” and has done nothing wrong. A spokesperson for Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. urged protesters on Sunday not to tarnish the country’s image amid the regional summit. “We should be uniting right at this time,” the spokesperson said. “Let’s not mar the Philippines’ image with other nations.” But the brutal crackdown on protesters has only urged more Filipinos to take to the streets, according to leaders of the protest movement, who estimated more than 10,000 would show up as the U.S. President landed in Manila. In response, police beefed up their security presence at one of the protest sites. “We want the whole world to see the protests Filipinos have prepared,” civic group leader Raymond Palatino told a local radio station earlier Tuesday. “If Marcos has a red-carpet welcome for Trump, for us, it’s protests.” The protests, however, are not necessarily representative of the Philippine population’s view of Trump. A Pew Research Survey conducted in February and March found that 68% of respondents in the country had confidence in Trump to do the right thing regarding world affairs—a greater share than those who had confidence in other world leaders, including France’s Emmanuel Macron, China’s Xi Jinping, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. How the AI revolution sparked protests Protesters have decried Trump’s role in exacerbating conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed energy and general goods prices upward globally. But at the heart of the Philippines protests is a U.S.-led initiative called Pax Silica , which draws from the Latin word pax for peace and aims to boost semiconductor and other supply chains to rival China’s growing AI and tech industry. Harkening to the “ Pax Americana ” period of relative peace post-World War II, the initiative, which was established in December 2025, has more than two dozen signatories , including the Philippines. Each of the signatories is expected to bring something to the table. The U.S. recognizes that the Philippines has “significant” reserves of minerals necessary for these chains. A note published by the ASEAN Business Advisory Council said the Philippines is a “critical production hub” that specializes in chip assembly, testing, and packaging, with the semiconductor and electronics sector remaining “the most significant contributor to the Philippines’ export performance.” Government figures show these accounted for 59.3% of Philippine merchandise exports in 2025. The Philippines’ participation would draw it into Washington’s AI arms race with Beijing, which Manila already has tensions with over disputes in the hotly contested South China Sea . The Marcos Administration wants to transform the Philippines into a regional AI powerhouse, and Finance Secretary Frederick Go said in April that, by joining Pax Silica, the country ensures that its “mineral resources and strategic location are not simply supporting global industries from the margins, but are actively harnessed to build the industries of the future.” In a July national address, Marcos touted that the initiative will “bring quality jobs to our people, accelerate our industrial competitiveness, and revitalize our economy.” Part of that initiative, however, is a plan to build an industrial hub covering an area greater than 3,000 football fields in New Clark City, north of Manila, which is close to the former U.S. Clark airbase . That land would also cover areas that generations of an Indigenous Aeta community have long inhabited as well as arable land that local farmers have long tilled. Human Rights Watch said Monday that the move threatens to displace these communities. “What will happen to our ancestral land?” a member of the Aeta community told local news outlet ABS-CBN on Monday. “They will just send us away? Kick us out? What will happen to our community?” Critics have also warned that building the hub threatens to consume the Philippines’ water, energy, and mineral resources—up to 90 million liters of water a day, based on officials’ estimates —and would stress the environment. This has fueled speculation that a data center is being built. The Philippines denied this , but a U.S. State Department spokesperson told the New York Times that it “will depend on a number of factors, including environmental and infrastructure studies still to come.” A farmers’ activist group criticized the plan in April, saying that the Philippines “is opening up our mountains and ancestral lands for destructive mining and foreign industries, not for Filipinos.” Philippine government happier to receive Despite reinvigorated U.S.-Philippines ties since Marcos’ presidency, Trump has made his dislike of multilateral forums well known, and the ASEAN Summit has historically been criticized for its lack of effectiveness and purpose. But the Philippine government appeared to make multiple accommodations for the U.S. President to visit, while on his way to the more significant Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders Meeting in Shenzhen—where he is set to meet with Putin and Xi later in the week. Even though Trump would miss most of the ASEAN leaders’ summit by the time he arrived on Tuesday, he would have missed even more had the Philippines’ foreign affairs department not intervened. The department told local paper BusinessMirror that it revised the original schedule, which was supposed to open two days earlier , to make it more amenable to leaders expected to attend other major international gatherings. Marcos is scheduled to receive Trump at the Philippine presidential palace on Wednesday, complete with a state banquet. Officials are also trying to wrangle a reunion between Trump and former Philippine First Lady Imelda Marcos , the current President’s 97-year-old mother. But that depends on whether doctors clear her to be fit. Authorities in Manila conducted road clearing and clean-up operations ahead of the summit, though critics argue that this was “ all for show ” and is an attempt to conceal the urban poor living in the capital’s streets. Marcos needs to woo Trump, Manila-based political analyst Cleve Arguelles, founder and CEO of public opinion research firm Momentum Research, tells TIME. Arguelles says that Marcos wants “to convince Trump personally that the Philippines is a valuable ally worth defending and investing in,” especially as the world becomes increasingly split between the U.S. and its adversaries. Arguelles adds that pleasing Trump could also give Marcos a chance to improve his domestic political authority, which has flagged amid an ongoing feud with his Vice President Sara Duterte , as well as reframe his family’s controversial legacy . “The Marcos family’s political rehabilitation has always had an international dimension, particularly given the role of the United States in facilitating the family’s departure from power in 1986,” Arguelles said. Marcos’ despotic father, who was the country’s former President from 1965 to 1986, was ousted by Filipinos in a popular revolt , and the U.S. helped their family leave the Philippines for Hawaii, where they lived in exile for a few years. Trump’s visit to the Philippines would be the first during his second-term administration, and Arguelles says that alone is already significant: “We should not underestimate the symbolic importance of an American President being warmly received by a Marcos.”

items.author: Jim Farber
items.title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
items.summary: Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that this physical media holds. Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic . “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.”

items.originalTitle: The Greenland Test: What Follows When America Coerces Its Allies
items.author: Ariane Tabatabai and John Drennan
items.title: The Greenland Test: What Follows When America Coerces Its Allies
items.summary: The US military's Pituffik Space Base on March 28, 2025 in Pituffik, Greenland. —Jim Watson-Pool-Getty Images President Donald Trump began his second term in office by weaponizing European worries about being abandoned by the United States, attacking NATO , and threatening to annex or buy Greenland , the semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. On Sept. 22, Trump got much of what he wanted, short of sovereignty. He signed an agreement with Denmark and Greenland on the future of U.S. presence on the island. In a speech at the United Nations, Trump described the deal as offering the U.S. “permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory,” and forbidding American adversaries from establishing a “military presence” or making “sensitive investments” there. The deal aims to address the limitations of the 1951 agreement that governed the U.S. security relationship with Greenland and counter the growing threat posed by Russian and Chinese activity in the Arctic. The new agreement increases American presence on the island through the expansion of two military installations. Whether it adequately addresses U.S. national security concerns remains to be seen. But it does resolve one of the disputes that have strained relations within NATO since President Trump’s return to office. And it reflects America’s short-term approach to coercing allies in the Trump Era. For now, the acute phase of the Greenland crisis appears to be over. Denmark’s ambassador to the U.N. described the deal as “good” for all parties, as well as for “international peace and security.” Some observers, irrespective of their views on the methods used to secure the agreement, have emphasized that the deal does advance U.S. national security interests. As Americans voted in midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress, Greenland’s legislature approved the September agreement . Trump hailed the Greenland deal as Europe giving the U.S. the “ greatest gift we were ever given .” Seventy years earlier, another American election coincided with a crisis between Washington and two of its closest allies, Britain and France, over their invasion of Egypt and seizure of the Suez Canal. Washington coerced its allies to withdraw their forces. Judged by its immediate aims, the coercion succeeded. But the longer-term costs of American coercion of allies offer a warning. Even if the Greenland crisis remains resolved ­, a big if , the consequences of Washington’s coercion, like those of its intervention in the Suez crisis, are likely to reverberate throughout the alliance for years to come. The historical parallels are imperfect, but earlier episodes of U.S. coercion against allies offer clues to what might follow. The U.S. has occasionally used coercion to resolve disagreements with allies. When it has, Washington has typically made its demands and their limits clear: it specified the policy outcome it sought, confined its pressure to the issue at hand, and promised a return to normal relations once the allies complied. In short, Washington offered a path back. The American nuclear non-proliferation policy illustrates this approach. In the 1970s, the U.S. used threats of abandonment, among other forms of pressure, to prevent South Korea from developing a nuclear weapons program. The Trump Administration’s coercion has typically lacked those limits. Its pressure spills across policy areas, from trade relationships to state sovereignty. What's more, it often lacks a clear, stated objective and offers no obvious path back. The administration has yet to articulate a positive vision for America’s alliances. In these ways, coercion under Trump differs in kind from that wielded by his predecessors. The resulting damage to America’s alliances is likely to endure long after the immediate disputes are settled. Ghosts of the past Even cases of conditional American coercion show how alliance cohesion can shift in ways the U.S. did not anticipate. In July 1956, President Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt proclaimed , “The Suez Canal belongs to us! And it will be run by Egyptians! Egyptians! Egyptians!” Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company, the international enterprise that had operated the canal since 1869. In the fall of 1956, as President Dwight Eisenhower campaigned for a second term, Britain partnered with France and Israel, invaded Egypt, and seized the northern end of the Suez Canal , a lucrative and vital waterway for international trade. The invasion of Egypt by American allies came at the height of the Cold War. The Eisenhower Administration worried about Soviet intervention in the Mediterranean should the conflict become prolonged, and Eisenhower wrote in his memoirs about the potential damage to the “interests of the entire Free World.” President Eisenhower launched a coercive campaign against Britain and France with the aims of establishing a ceasefire and then the withdrawal from Egypt. In the aftermath of World War II, Britain was heavily indebted, and the pound’s role as an international reserve currency made it vulnerable to a run. The British pound came under pressure. Washington squeezed Britain’s finances and oil supply until its allies agreed first to stop their military campaign and then to withdraw from Egypt. Britain accepted a ceasefire on Nov. 6, the day of the U.S. presidential election, and France, unable to continue without its ally, followed. George Humphrey, who was the Secretary of the Treasury at the time, told the British ambassador, “You are like burglars who have broken into somebody else’s house. So get out! When you do, not until then, you’ll get help.” Only once London announced the withdrawal in December did relief follow, including a large IMF drawing. The withdrawal of French and British forces from Egypt came to symbolize their decline as imperial powers. Washington saw its coercive campaign as a success. Britain and France halted their operations within days and withdrew their forces by Dec. 1956. But over time, the episode propelled the two countries along divergent paths: Britain deepened its reliance on the U.S., and France sought greater autonomy. The different British and French strategic choices were shaped by the options each country had and whether backing down discredited only a leader or an entire policy direction. Britain already had the bomb, having conducted its first nuclear test in 1952, but nuclear weapons could not protect against the financial pressure Washington had applied. And Britain had already walked away from the negotiations on European integration in 1955. With no other alternatives to fall back on, it chose to rebuild its standing in Washington, a bet that paid off with the 1958 U.S.-U.K. Mutual Defense Agreement. In London, backing down cost Prime Minister Anthony Eden his job, but left his party in power to double down on the relationship with Washington. In Paris, where the invasion had broad support, capitulation discredited an entire policy direction. France also had alternatives: a nuclear program underway and a European path with a willing partner in West Germany. The French turn toward Europe gained urgency on Nov. 6, 1956. West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer was in Paris that day to discuss the European project; his meeting with French Prime Minister Guy Mollet gave momentum to the negotiations that produced the Treaty of Rome the following March. “ Europe will be your revenge ,” the West German leader told the French, according to Christian Pineau, France’s foreign minister at the time. Within a decade of Suez, France had also tested its first nuclear weapon and announced its withdrawal from NATO’s integrated military command. These policies survived the collapse of France’s Fourth Republic and the advent of its Fifth Republic, as France continued to pursue greater independence from the U.S. Two decades after the crisis, Pineau, hardly an impartial observer, wrote that the French public backed Charles de Gaulle’s withdrawal from NATO’s integrated military command because the French people had “lost confidence” in American commitments. In his view, the French felt abandoned by Eisenhower. “The Suez affair had made the French forget the amphibious invasion of Normandy and the Marshall Plan,” Pineau observed. The price of American coercion President Trump antagonized America’s closest allies during his first term, but he has intensified his coercive campaigns against them since returning to the White House in January 2025. His threats to acquire Greenland led the Danish government to plan to blow up runways on the island and fly in additional supplies of blood in preparation for a possible American invasion. Trump has spoken about making Canada the 51st state of the U.S., signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America, levied a series of tariffs , and has banned several Canadian products. He has done so with constantly shifting rationale and no clear path for restoring the bilateral relationship. It is too early to know the lasting consequences of these coercive campaigns. Although Denmark ultimately reached a deal with the United States, the way it weathered the crisis is telling. Copenhagen built a European coalition around Greenland, with military personnel from Finland, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the United Kingdom deploying alongside Danish forces, and France opening a consulate on the island. Canada may already be following the path of greater autonomy from America that the French took after Suez, although it is yet unclear whether that shift will outlast the immediate dispute, survive a change in leadership in Washington or Ottawa, or endure over time. Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada is already hedging. Ottawa signed a security and defense partnership with the European Union in June 2025. In February, Canada became the first non-European country to join SAFE, the European Union’s €150 billion ($164 billion) loan program for defense procurement. Canadian officials have framed the decision partly as a way to secure market access for Canadian industry, but the direction of travel is clear. Many American allies today resemble France of the 1950s and the 1960s more than Britain in ways that matter most. They have both a motive to hedge and partners—often targets of U.S. coercion themselves—willing to hedge with them. In 1956, “Europe” was a nascent project. Now, it is an institution with its own defense funds and procurement programs. In the 1950s and 1960s, American allies had few alternatives in a bipolar world. Today, changes in the global balance of power are testing American predominance and could offer these allies new partners, including China. And much as de Gaulle pursued closer ties with the Soviet Union in the 1960s without leaving the Western camp, American allies need not shift the center of gravity of their foreign policies toward China. Carney, who described China as the biggest security threat to Canada during his 2025 campaign, traveled to Beijing in January 2026, cut tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, and spoke of China as a more predictable partner . Not every ally will follow that course. Allies that depend most directly on U.S. forces for their survival may hedge more slowly, if at all. The result could be a divided alliance network, with some members hedging against American power and others continuing to hang on. American coercion during the Suez crisis directly targeted two allies, but it also sent a signal to others. West Germany watched as the U.S. mounted a sustained economic and political pressure campaign against two of its closest allies. In Pineau’s telling , Adenauer shared his French counterparts’ doubts about American guarantees and urged them to focus on European integration. Today, the entire network of American allies is watching as the Trump Administration subjects one friend after another to coercion. The European deployments to Greenland suggest that some are already drawing conclusions and acting on them. One can draw some comfort from NATO’s survival despite the tensions that have strained the alliance since Trump returned to office. But France did not formally leave NATO after the Suez crisis. It scaled back its role within the alliance. In a decade, the U.S. may find that its allies remain bound to it on paper but have so thoroughly hedged against American power that America’s leverage and influence have fundamentally eroded. Once upon a time, America had a vast network of allies and partners whose capabilities it could draw on, whose markets it could access on cooperative terms, and whose support it could count on in a crisis or war. America might now find itself increasingly alone. Some of this hedging will likely be reversible, especially if the new Congress takes a more active role in foreign policy and checks an administration that indiscriminately coerces allies to secure short-term, transactional goals. But some of the damage will outlast both the Greenland crisis and the Trump Administration. Diplomatic warmth can return with a new administration, as it did when Joe Biden became president in 2021. But procurement programs, supply chains, and institutional commitments such as SAFE, with provisions favoring European suppliers , can bind allies to new partners for years to come. Future American administrations seeking to repair these relationships will be forced to compete for the loyalty of their allies. They will not be able to simply reclaim it.

items.originalTitle: Congressman Says U.S. Gets Threats ‘Quite Often’ Amid Reports of Iran Plotting ‘Dirty Bomb’
items.author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
items.title: Congressman Says U.S. Gets Threats ‘Quite Often’ Amid Reports of Iran Plotting ‘Dirty Bomb’
items.summary: A person waves an Iranian national flag in front of an anti-U.S. billboard depicting President Donald Trump in prison, during a nightly rally in downtown Tehran, Iran, on Nov. 5, 2026. —Morteza Nikoubazl—NurPhoto/Getty Images Iran is reportedly developing potential plans to detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington, D.C., a threat that one member of the House Intelligence Committee called an intimidation tactic. Citing seven U.S. officials, CNN reported on Monday that new U.S. intelligence indicates planning by Iran to target Trump Administration officials in an attack on the capital. Intelligence reportedly also intercepted Iranian chatter claiming to have stashed bomb-making materials inside the U.S., although officials disagree about the credibility of that claim. Such an attack would be a major escalation. Since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran on Feb. 28, Iran has attacked U.S. military bases in the Middle East, as well as energy facilities , commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz , and U.S. allies in the Gulf . But it has not launched a direct attack on American soil. U.S. officials reportedly see the intelligence as a sign that Iran may be eyeing escalation amid stalled negotiations. But U.S. officials said intelligence does not necessarily indicate an imminent threat, and they are still assessing whether Iran could or would carry out such an attack. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to CNN that the U.S. is “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.” TIME has reached out to the White House and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which the Defense Department referred to, for comment. Representative André Carson (D, Ind.) told CNN on Monday that the House Intelligence Committee gets “these kinds of reports quite often,” but many do not become public. An official told CNN that Iran is cognizant of the risk of retaliation if it were to attack the U.S. Nevertheless, the report raises questions about U.S. preparedness against an attack using an unconventional weapon. It would be “extremely easy,” one official reportedly said, for operatives to have entered the U.S. over the past decade and pre-positioned bomb components or nuclear materials within the country. Officials have reportedly discussed countermeasures against the potential threat in Washington, and contingency planning against threats in the Middle East. Attorney General Todd Blanche last week urged congressional leaders to reauthorize a national security law that allows U.S. authorities to surveil foreign nationals abroad. Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act expired in June, although existing surveillance orders remain valid until March 2027. The New York Times reported on Nov. 3 that Israel had shared intelligence suggesting Iran was considering using chemical weapons against its adversaries, an assessment that divided U.S. officials. Officials told CNN that American troops in the Middle East would not have adequate protection or training in the event of such an attack. A spokesperson for the Iranian Mission at the United Nations in New York rejected the allegations of chemical weapons planning. Iran “considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be wholly illegitimate and categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations circulated in this regard,” the spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. What is a ‘dirty bomb’? A dirty bomb is a weapon that combines a conventional explosive, like dynamite or TNT, with radioactive material. It is not a nuclear weapon and its explosion is millions of times less powerful than an atomic bomb. While a detonated nuclear weapon spreads radiation across thousands of square miles, a dirty bomb could scatter radioactive debris over a few blocks or miles. It takes relatively little expertise to build a dirty bomb, according to the Council on Foreign Relations . “No special assembly is required; the regular explosive simply disperses the radioactive material packed into the bomb,” CFR writes. “The hardest part is acquiring the radioactive material, not building the bomb.” But CFR notes that not all dirty bombs are equally dangerous. How much damage it can do depends on access to sophisticated technologies needed to handle highly radioactive material. Most of the danger from a dirty bomb comes from the initial explosion, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . The radioactive materials scattered by a dirty bomb are unlikely to produce enough radiation exposure to cause immediate serious illness, except to those very close to the blast site, the CDC says. But the radioactive dust and smoke can still be dangerous if inhaled, and the CDC recommends covering your nose and mouth with a cloth if you are outside or in a car near the explosion site, and entering a nearby building where the walls and windows have not been broken. Avoid touching any objects thrown off by the explosion, and once you are indoors, shut all windows, remove and seal your outer layer of clothing in a plastic bag, and shower with soap and water. Experts sometimes point to the radiological accident in Goiânia, Brazil, in 1987 as an illustration of the potential consequences of radioactive contamination. On Sept. 13, 1987, scavengers broke into an abandoned private radiotherapy clinic and removed part of a teletherapy machine containing a cesium-137 source. The capsule was punctured days later, exposing cesium chloride that emitted a blue glow. Unaware of the danger, people rubbed the powder on their skin and shared it with others over two weeks. Four people died from radiation exposure. More than 100,000 people were screened after the hazard was identified, and 249 were found to have radioactive contamination. Authorities oversaw extensive environmental remediation, including the demolition of multiple homes. Has a dirty bomb been used before? Never has a dirty bomb been detonated in an attack before, although there have been several attempts and plots to use one. Iraq tested a one-ton radiological bomb in 1987, according to CFR, but found that the radiation levels it generated were too weak to make the weapon effective. In what a chronology compiled by PBS describes as “the first-ever attempt at radiological terror,” Chechen rebels in November 1995 told a Russian TV station that they planted a cache of radioactive material in Moscow’s Izmailovsky Park. A TV crew located a partially buried container holding cesium-137 in the park. Authorities removed the container and no explosion occurred. In 2002, the U.S. arrested Jose Padilla, an American citizen and alleged al-Qaeda operative, on suspicion of plotting to build and detonate a dirty bomb in a U.S. city. Padilla was arrested in Chicago after he returned from Pakistan, and designated an enemy combatant. He was held in military custody for more than three years without formal criminal charges. The government omitted the “dirty bomb” allegations from his 2005 indictment in civilian court, but he was convicted in 2007 of terrorism-related offences. He was released on Nov. 12 after serving nearly 21 years in prison after his indictment. In October 2022, eight months after invading Ukraine, Russian officials accused Ukraine of preparing to detonate a dirty bomb in what they said would be a false-flag attack to blame Moscow. Ukraine rejected the allegations, and Western officials warned that Russia would use the claims as a pretext for an escalation. Ukraine formally requested an inspection by the International Atomic Energy Agency, which found no sign of undeclared nuclear activity or materials at three locations inspected. Previous Iranian threats to the U.S. The reported planning suggests Iran is considering expanding its methods to include radiological or chemical attacks, but it’s not the first time Iran has planned or attempted an attack within the U.S. U.S. prosecutors have charged members and associates of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in multiple alleged plots to assassinate people on American soil. U.S. intelligence has also flagged other suspected Iranian plans for attacks. Prosecutors have brought multiple cases since the war began more than eight months ago. On Nov. 10, federal prosecutors in Manhattan announced an expanded indictment against three men—Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani—accused of orchestrating attacks for groups linked to the IRGC and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kata’ib Hizballah. The allegations include 18 attacks and attempted attacks in Europe, a plot to bomb a Manhattan synagogue, and a September plot against a British air base housing U.S. personnel . Last week, the Secret Service reportedly moved Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into military housing because of threats to his life that were linked to Iran. Bessent has led the Trump Administration’s sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran that has crippled the country’s economy alongside a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports . In February, an FBI bulletin circulated, suggesting that Iran was considering launching drones from a vessel offshore against targets in California if the U.S. attacked Iran. No such attack followed the U.S. strikes, and the White House later said the warning rested on a single unverified tip. Iranian state media have also circulated threats against President Donald Trump and his family . In 2024, U.S. authorities also accused Iran of two assassination plots targeting Trump. In one, Pakistani national Asif Merchant sought to hire undercover officers posing as hitmen to kill Trump. He was convicted in March. In the other, prosecutors alleged that an IRGC official instructed Afghan national Farhad Shakeri in October 2024 to develop a plan to kill Trump. Neither plot resulted in an attack. Iran has been linked to several other assassinations and plots in the U.S. In July 1980, Iranian dissident and former diplomat Ali Akbar Tabatabai was murdered at his home in Bethesda, Md. Dawud Salahuddin later admitted to killing him at the behest of the Iranian government. In 2011, U.S. authorities disrupted a plot to assassinate Saudi Ambassador Adel al-Jubeir by bombing a restaurant in Washington, D.C. Manssor Arbabsiar pleaded guilty to conspiring with Iranian Quds Force officials to kill the ambassador, and was sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2013. In 2021, IRGC member Shahram Poursafi allegedly offered $300,000 to arrange the murder of former national security adviser John Bolton in Washington or Maryland, in apparent retaliation for the U.S. killing of Iranian General Qassem Soleimani . And in 2023, the Justice Department charged two men allegedly linked to the IRGC with a murder-for-hire plot against Masih Alinejad, an Iranian-American journalist and critic of Iran’s government. Two organizers were convicted in March 2025 for the 2022 plot. Neither target was killed. As for the latest threat, Representative Carson characterized it as a desperate intimidation tactic by Iran. “They’re trying to level the playing field by sending out this threat,” he said, characterizing Iran’s leaders as “losing their grip.”
